chapter_theme: The third part of the debate with Kundalakesi: Neelakesi mocks her opponent and her teacher, denies the Buddha omniscience and so scriptural authority, reduces the five aggregates to knowing and form, and argues through a run of images (the self-binding thief, the soldier who reports his own death, the garland thread, the scented pot) that momentariness and continuity without a soul cannot stand; Kundalakesi then turns to the Buddha's birth-stories of giving his eyes, body, wife and child, and Neelakesi answers that such gifts are madness, meet no need, and make the testing god ignorant.

cast.role: the demoness of the burning-ground temple who takes the Jain dharma and becomes its debater
the Buddhist woman debater whom Neelakesi answers
those sitting near who hear the debate

192.reading: Neelakesi laughs that the Buddhists' leader tore open his mother's side at his birth while himself feeling no pain, and that this woman on the dark hill threw down her own husband; who else on earth, she asks, walks so great a path with so great a compassion as these two.
192.nuance: The praise is mockery: பெருவழியார் பேரருளார் is turned against the two whose compassion the Buddhists would claim. The first half refers to a birth that harmed the mother, the second to Kundalakesi's killing of her husband on the hill; the verse names neither story more than this, and காலனையும் (her husband, 'Death' himself?) is hard to fix. The jibe attacks persons, not doctrine, and so carries no claim.
192.event: Neelakesi mocks Kundalakesi with her teacher's birth and her own killing of her husband.

193.reading: Neelakesi tells Kundalakesi that her leader does not know all things without remainder, since he knew only through the eye and the other organs, by seeing, hearing and reasoning, like a man who merely carries a load, and asks whether the word of one without subtle knowledge can be scripture.
193.nuance: The argument ties a book's authority to its author's omniscience: what the Buddhists count as the means of knowledge (sense and inference) is here made a limit, so a teacher who used them cannot be the all-knower the Jain invocation (verse 1) makes the mark of god. The simile of the load-bearer (இலை சுமக்கும் ஒருவன்) is not fully clear.

claims.claim: the Buddha did not know all things, since he knew only through the senses, hearing and reasoning
only the word of one with complete and subtle knowledge can count as scripture

194.reading: Neelakesi argues that to speak of five aggregates is an error: feeling, perception and volition are not other than knowing and are one with it, so with form there are only two, and in saying more Kundalakesi has stopped speaking of aggregates and arrived at real principles.
194.nuance: The Buddhist list in Manimekalai 30 is form, feeling, perception, formation and consciousness (உருவு நுகர்ச்சி குறிப்பே பாவனை உள்ள அறிவு); the Neelakesi's terms (குறி, உழப்பு, செய்கை) are close but its own, and its reduction to knowing and form mirrors the Jain pair of soul and non-soul. Line 2's சிங்குந்தன் is obscure, so which three are merged is a reading.

claims.claim: a person is made of five aggregates
feeling, perception and volition are modes of knowing, so the aggregates reduce to knowing and form

195.reading: Neelakesi calls it great folly to say that each thing first perishes wholly and that another knowledge arises after that total destruction, likening it to saying that a man who came in yesterday at midnight handed himself over, took me, and went away.
195.nuance: The absurd tale makes one who has ceased the agent of an exchange: if the earlier moment is wholly gone it cannot pass anything to the later one. The joke turns on the same person being both giver and taken.

claims.claim: each moment perishes wholly and a different cognition arises after it

196.reading: Like a thief who is also the one who binds himself, Neelakesi says, if the mind perishes utterly together with what it knew and not a sesame seed of it remains, how can perishing itself be known; she bids the clear-minded woman think it over calmly.
196.nuance: The thief-and-captor image charges the doctrine with needing the perished mind to witness its own end. தெள்ளியாய் ('clear one') is courteous in form and ironic in force.

claims.claim: the mind perishes entirely together with what it knew
if nothing of the mind remains, no one is left to know its perishing

197.reading: Neelakesi compares Kundalakesi to a soldier who, while king, general and champion fall and he himself flees, says 'I was killed': she speaks while bound, and the verse asks whether one who has fallen tells his own fall to the fallen.
197.nuance: A battlefield report serves as a figure for the momentary self reporting its own extinction: speech about total perishing presupposes a speaker who did not perish.

claims.claim: what has perished cannot report its own perishing

198.reading: Neelakesi says that if one cites the birth of the crescent moon and the birth of children, hidden things become plain; she asks what is lacking, and whether the birth Kundalakesi described on this earth should be taken as a principle.
198.nuance: The verse seems to answer an example the Buddhist used for birth without a continuing self (the moon renewed, the child born), but lines 2 and 3 (மறைபொருள்கள் வெளிப்பட்டா, வான்வயிற்றால்) are obscure and the argument cannot be fixed.

claims.claim: the birth the Buddhist describes cannot be taken as a real principle

199.reading: Neelakesi says that Kundalakesi has spent long hours expounding two kinds of continuum, the separate and the unseparated, and asks whether, if they serve only to destroy without trace the meaning of all she said, her case does not collapse.
199.nuance: பின்ன சந்தானம் and பிறிதில் சந்தானம் name the Buddhist series of moments as the Neelakesi reports them; the Buddhist sources here do not use these terms. Line 4 (ஆதனாழிநாட் டாகாதோ) is obscure and the conclusion is a guess.

claims.claim: there are two kinds of continuum, the separate and the unseparated

200.reading: If the countless aggregates follow without interval, Neelakesi argues, either they never meet and so stay unmixed, or, if their unbroken succession means they touch, two become one; either way the lord's complete extinction becomes hard to hold.
200.nuance: The dilemma is aimed at release as total cessation (அறக்கேடு): a series that either never joins or fuses leaves no clean end. The reading of line 2 (கண்ணுறாது ஒன்றுதலால்) is uncertain.

claims.claim: countless aggregates follow one another without interval
an unbroken series of aggregates cannot end in the teacher's complete extinction

201.reading: Even if knowledge is carried on by traces, Neelakesi argues, if nothing at all of the first moment is in the one that follows, knowing and speaking become impossible; and if something is there, then like the thread inside a great garland she has described a soul stretched longer than a league.
201.nuance: The garland image is the core of the Jain answer: what runs unbroken through the flowers is the soul the Buddhist denies. The league (ஓசனை) is mockery of a self drawn out across all its moments.

claims.claim: memory and knowledge are carried from moment to moment by traces
whatever carries the traces through the moments is a soul, as the thread runs through a garland

202.reading: Neelakesi asks whether Kundalakesi's principle is that the scent of the pathiri flower stays undestroyed in the new pot even after the flower decays, and argues that then, as the scent outlasts the flower, the soul too should outlast the perishing body.
202.nuance: The image of the new pot scented by pathiri flowers was evidently the Buddhist's example for traces that pass on without a substance; Neelakesi turns it to show something that endures. Line 4 (முடிவு உயிர்க்கே ஆகாதோ) can also be read as a question whether the soul too must end, which would reverse the point.

claims.claim: traces persist as the pathiri scent stays in a new pot after the flower is gone
as the scent outlasts the flower, the soul outlasts the body

203.reading: If Kundalakesi says that a power passed across, Neelakesi argues, that power is a sixth thing besides the five aggregates; and if it is nothing besides the five, then, mad one, she has after all spoken of total destruction.
203.nuance: The dilemma closes the run on momentariness: either something beyond the aggregates (a self in all but name) or total destruction with nothing to carry deeds or knowledge. பித்தியாய் is a direct insult.

claims.claim: a power passes from one moment of the aggregates to the next
such a power is either a sixth thing beyond the five aggregates or there is total destruction

204.reading: As those sitting near think that Neelakesi has raised many waves of argument, Kundalakesi resolves to establish that the faults laid on her leader's scripture, its meaning and his life have no ground, and sets out to tell what her leader did.
204.nuance: The debate turns here from doctrine to the teacher's life (நிகழ்ச்சி): having lost the argument on momentariness, the Buddhist defends by the founder's conduct. The order of lines 3 and 4 makes the subject of நிறுத்துவன் யான் Kundalakesi speaking.
204.event: The onlookers judge Neelakesi's case strong, and Kundalakesi undertakes to defend her teacher's scripture and life.

claims.claim: the Buddha's scripture, its meaning and his conduct are free of fault

205.reading: Kundalakesi tells of her teacher's former gifts: he gave his eyes, gave his flesh, gave himself to a tiger, gave his wife, split open his body and gave it to others, gave land and gave his child, and to those who came to him he gave heaven; she bids Neelakesi listen while she tells them in full.
205.nuance: These are the birth-stories (சாதகம், 206) of the bodhisattva's total giving, offered as proof of compassion. The gift of wife and child is listed with the gifts of the body without comment. Neelakesi answers the catalogue in 207 to 210 by calling such giving madness and its test by Indra empty.
205.event: Kundalakesi recites the Buddha's gifts in former births.

claims.claim: the Buddha's gifts in former births of his eyes, body, wife, child and land prove his compassion

206.reading: Saying that these are the birth-stories of 'our lord who removes the distress of strangers', Kundalakesi with long garlanded hair told them one after another for the whole length of a day.
206.nuance: ஏதிலார் இடர் தீர்க்கும் (who ends the distress of those who are nothing to him) names compassion for strangers as the teacher's mark. Line 3 (யோகினாணின்று) is unclear: perhaps she stood in her practice.
206.event: Kundalakesi recites the birth-stories for a whole day.

claims.claim: the Buddha removes the distress even of those who are strangers to him

207.reading: Neelakesi of the long eyes answers that the Buddha's story Kundalakesi told is like the doings of the deluded and the possessed.
207.nuance: The Jain answer does not deny the stories but judges them: gifts of one's own eyes, flesh and family are not compassion but disorder. Line 1 (நூலும் நாரும் இசைத்தன ஒத்தலால்) is unclear; it may say that her words matched as thread and fibre are twisted together.
207.event: Neelakesi dismisses the birth-stories as the deeds of the mad.

claims.claim: giving away one's eyes, body, wife and child is the conduct of the deluded and the possessed, not of the compassionate

208.reading: People who live their lives do not come asking 'give us slices of flesh, eyes, heads and meat at once'; would anyone go to a gruel-seller to get such things, Neelakesi asks.
208.nuance: The objection is from use: a gift must answer a real need, and no one needs another's eyes or head. கூழன் (the gruel-man) seems to be the ordinary giver of food, set against the giver of his body.

claims.claim: gifts of one's flesh, eyes and head meet no real need, since no living person asks for them

209.reading: As for the splitting of the body and the rest, Neelakesi says, if Indra came to test the giver he would know the man's heart; if he could not discern another's mind, to speak of him as a god is merely to claim a title.
209.nuance: The birth-stories in which a god comes in disguise to ask for the bodhisattva's body are attacked from the side of the tester: a god who must test does not know, and the test itself proves nothing a true knower needed. The close (ஓர் கிழமையும் போலுமே) is uncertain.

claims.claim: a god who must test a giver to learn his heart cannot read minds and is god only in name

210.reading: Whoever the asker may be, Neelakesi argues, since no ordinary man would ask such a thing the giver will see that he is a god; and having seen it, the wish to give will arise with no fear that he will die.
210.nuance: If the giver recognises the divine asker, the sacrifice is safe and its merit void: the gift is made in the expectation of no loss. Taking அன்னவன் இன்மையின் as 'since no such man exists' is a reading.

claims.claim: a giver who knows the asker is a god gives without risk of death, so the gift is no sacrifice

211.reading: Indra does not think that one without firm knowledge reaches an end, Neelakesi says, and since there is no answer to this, she asks the jewelled woman where she will find a way to join the earlier and later parts of her story.
211.nuance: Line 1 (உறுதி யல்லதுணர்வடையான்றனக) and line 3 (மறுதி) are hard to construe; the verse seems to say the birth-stories cannot be made consistent with the god's testing. The reading is tentative throughout.

links.note: The invocation praises as god only the one who knows all (எல்லா முணர்ந்தான்); verse 193 denies that the Buddha knew without remainder (ஒழிவின்றி யுணர்கலான்).
links.teaches: The invocation's definition of god by omniscience is not only praise but the premise of the debate: it becomes the test by which the rival teacher's book is ruled out as scripture.

links.note: The Buddhist teacher in the Manimekalai accepts only two means of knowledge, perception and inference; Neelakesi says a teacher who knew only through the senses and reasoning lacks subtle knowledge and his word is no scripture.
links.teaches: The same restriction to perception and inference that the Buddhist offers as rigour is, from the Jain side, the proof that its founder was not omniscient and so cannot ground a scripture.

links.note: The Manimekalai names the five aggregates (form, feeling, perception, formation, consciousness); Neelakesi says three of them are modes of knowing, leaving two.
links.teaches: Set beside the Buddhist's own list, the Jain attack is seen to aim at the split of consciousness from feeling, perception and volition, collapsing the person into a knower and form, which is the Jain soul and matter by another route.

links.note: The Manimekalai's teacher says the mind arises like lightning (சித்தம் உற்பவித்தது மின்போல்); Neelakesi asks how, if the mind perishes wholly with what it knew, its perishing could be known.
links.teaches: The Buddhist offers the lightning-flash mind as a manner of speaking about what has no lasting being, while the Jain treats it as a claim about a knower and asks who is left to witness the flash's end.

links.note: The Manimekalai says the chain of becoming has no I and no mine, no going and no coming; Neelakesi says whatever carries traces across the moments is a soul, like the thread in a garland.
links.teaches: The point of disagreement is located exactly: both accept that something continues from moment to moment, and they differ only on whether that continuity needs a thread, a soul, running through it.

links.note: Both use the new pot that takes the scent of pathiri flowers: the Naladiyar for the unlearned who gain sense from the learned, the Neelakesi for the Buddhist example of traces that persist after the flower is gone.
links.teaches: A homely image of borrowed fragrance served Tamil writers for transmission without identity, and the Jain debater shows that the image cuts both ways, since a scent that outlives its flower can be claimed for an enduring soul.

gains.a: the Neelakesi's turn of the image is seen to work on a figure already proverbial in Tamil ethical verse
gains.b: the quatrain's simile is shown to carry a philosophical question it leaves unasked: whether what is passed on is something that lasts

links.note: The Kural says the loving belong to others even to their bones; Kundalakesi lists the Buddha's literal gifts of eyes, body, wife and child as proof of his compassion.
links.teaches: The couplet's figure of giving one's bones becomes in the birth-stories a literal record of bodily gifts, and the pairing shows where the figure turns contestable: once it includes wife and child, the Jain opponent can call it madness rather than love.

gains.a: the catalogue of gifts is seen as an extreme reading of a Tamil ideal of love, not a foreign oddity
gains.b: the couplet's hyperbole is shown being taken literally and so exposed to an objection it does not face on its own

links.note: The Kundalakesi invocation praises its lord as one who kept nothing for himself and laboured only for others' good; Neelakesi calls the stories of the Buddha's self-giving the doings of the deluded and possessed.
links.teaches: The Buddhist poem makes self-giving the very definition of its lord, so the Jain reply that such giving is madness strikes at the ground of the rival's devotion and not at a side issue.

links.note: Purananuru 43 praises a Chola as descendant of the king of limitless giving who entered the scales to save a dove from a hawk; Neelakesi says no living person asks for another's flesh, eyes or head.
links.teaches: The gift of one's own flesh to a creature in distress, a dynastic boast in Sangam praise and a credential of compassion for the Buddhist, is denied any worth by the Jain debater's test of need, so Tamil tradition did not hold it as a settled virtue.

gains.a: the debater's objection is seen to reject a gift that Tamil royal praise held up as the summit of bounty
gains.b: the poem's ancestral boast is shown to have met a reasoned challenge in a later work

new_concepts.gloss: the five aggregates (form, feeling, perception, formation, consciousness) that are spoken of as a person
new_concepts.label_source: the verse's own word: ஐங்கந்தம் (194), பலகந்தம் (200)

new_concepts.gloss: the Buddha: the awakened teacher of dharma, his coming in a dark age, and the worship of his seat and footprints
new_concepts.label_source: the verse's own word: புத்தர் சரிதை (207); elsewhere தலைவன் (192, 193, 204)

source_issues: 192 line 2: காலனையும் (her husband as 'Death'?) is hard to construe.
194 line 2: சிங்குந்தன் is obscure; the list of three aggregates may be corrupt.
198 lines 2-3: மறைபொருள்கள் வெளிப்பட்டா and வான்வயிற்றால் do not yield a clear argument.
199 line 4: ஆதனாழிநாட் டாகாதோ is obscure, possibly corrupt.
201 lines 3-4: the line break doubles ல் (போல் / லோசனை), a division error of the edition or e-text.
211 lines 1-2: the break doubles க (தனக / கிறுதி), and மறுதி in line 3 is obscure.
207 line 1: நூலு நாரு மிசைத்தன வொத்தலான் is unclear.
